planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and site a second seedling nearby for cross-pollination and better nut set.

directions: This small, often multi-stemmed Chinese chestnut species stays noticeably more compact and precocious than Castanea mollissima, bearing small but sweet nuts within a few years of planting. Its shrubby, blight-tolerant growth habit has made it useful as breeding stock and understock for dwarfing chestnut orchards. Grow in full sun on well-drained acidic soil and mulch to conserve moisture; prune out weak interior growth to keep the multi-trunked form open. Harvest the small spiny burs in autumn as they split and drop, and store nuts cool and slightly moist since they lose viability quickly if allowed to dry out.

planting.note: Plant in deep, well-drained soil away from gardens since roots exude juglone, and stake young trees in their first few seasons against wind.

directions: Native to the mountains of Yunnan and Guizhou in southwestern China, this species produces thick-shelled nuts so hard they are traditionally carved into decorative hand exercise balls, giving rise to the common name 'iron walnut.' It grows into a large, long-lived tree much like Juglans regia but tends to tolerate warmer, more humid summers better than the Persian walnut. Give it full sun, deep soil, and room to spread, and expect a long juvenile period before significant nut production begins. Nuts ripen in autumn and should be hulled promptly, then cured in a dry, ventilated spot for several weeks before cracking.

planting.note: Site in deep soil well away from vegetable beds due to juglone root exudate, and give it plenty of overhead room since the pinnate leaves can reach three feet long.

directions: This cold-hardy walnut from northeastern China, Korea, and the Russian Far East tolerates winters far colder than Juglans regia, making it a popular shade and nut tree in northern climates where Persian walnut fails. It bears small, thick-shelled nuts in clusters and has large, coarsely toothed compound leaves that give it a bold, tropical look in summer. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and allow room for its broad, spreading canopy to develop undisturbed. Hull and dry the nuts soon after they drop in fall, as the kernels are prone to rancidity if left in damp hulls too long.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade along a streambank or woodland edge, mimicking the wet bottomland forests of its native range.

directions: Discovered and formally described only in the early 2000s from a handful of bottomland forest sites in the Big Thicket region of East Texas and nearby Louisiana, this is one of the most recently recognized native North American witch hazel species. It is distinguished from its relatives by rounder, more oval leaves and unusual bronze-pink to dull red flowers that open in mid to late winter on bare stems. Give it consistently moist, acidic, organically rich soil in part shade, similar to the wet hardwood bottomlands where it naturally occurs. Because wild populations are extremely limited, plants grown from nursery-propagated stock are an important way to conserve this species in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil with good air circulation, since crowded or stressed trees become vulnerable to tip blight.

directions: This broad, dense pine from southern and central Europe has long been one of the most widely planted windbreak and street trees in North America thanks to its tolerance of wind, drought, poor soil, road salt, and urban pollution. Stiff, dark green needles in bundles of two and a pyramidal-to-rounded crown give it a coarser, bolder texture than native eastern white pine. Plant in full sun with good air movement, since older or stressed trees in humid regions can become susceptible to Diplodia tip blight and Dothistroma needle blight. Established trees need little supplemental water or fertilizer and are best left unpruned beyond removing dead wood.
